data.title: Nvidia vs. Alphabet: One AI Stock Is a Bargain, the Other Raises Red Flags, Says Investor
data.description:
It’s been a year Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) investors would prefer to forget. Despite delivering strong financial results, both companies have found themselves caught in a Wall Street sell-off driven by a near-perfect storm of political, regulatory, and financial concerns. The Democrats’ Blue Wave election victory has raised fears of tougher restrictions on AI development and data center construction, while the scandal surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, followed by his resignation, has shaken confidence in one of the industry’s most influential leaders.

And the problems don’t end there. China’s regulatory tensions have weighed on semiconductor stocks, while repeated attempts to stabilize the market have failed to stop the selling. Even Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO, initially seen as a potential turning point for the tech sector, failed to lift investor confidence, with the stock plunging just one day after its debut. Add mounting losses at investment funds, persistent inflation, and hawkish Federal Reserve commentary pointing toward higher interest rates, and investors have plenty of reasons to remain cautious.

But as legendary investor Warren Buffett has long argued, periods of widespread fear can also create opportunities to buy outstanding companies at discounted prices. The challenge, of course, is distinguishing between stocks that have become genuinely undervalued and those whose falling prices reflect deeper problems.

That brings us to Nvidia, Alphabet, and investor Gil Rotstein, who believes the recent sell-off has created a buying opportunity in one AI giant but exposed serious concerns about the other. After examining both companies, he sees a bargain in one stock and growing financial risks in its rival.

Starting with Nvidia, Rotstein believes investors are overlooking the chipmaker’s underlying financial strength as concerns surrounding its former CEO and Washington’s investigations dominate the conversation.

“Don’t be a fool and think Washington will let it drown,” Rotstein said.

Rotstein believes Nvidia’s importance to the broader tech industry and the enormous amount of computing infrastructure being built worldwide make it unlikely that Washington would take actions that could seriously damage the company. In his view, policymakers have strong incentives to protect a leading supplier of the hardware powering the AI revolution.

Valuation is another important consideration. According to Rotstein, Nvidia trades at less than 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, compared with 28.5 times for AMD and 17.6 times for Broadcom. He also points to the company’s remaining $227.3 billion share repurchase authorization, which could provide additional support for existing investors.

There are risks, particularly from regulatory investigations and competition from custom-designed processors. However, Rotstein believes the potential rewards outweigh those concerns, especially given Nvidia’s ability to maintain strong profitability across its integrated hardware and software offerings.

Ultimately, Rotstein rates Nvidia shares a Buy, viewing the gap between its operational performance and depressed valuation as an opportunity for patient investors. (To watch Rotstein’s track record, click here)

Alphabet presents a more complicated picture. Rotstein previously supported the Google parent’s investment prospects, but its latest quarterly results have prompted him to reconsider whether the company’s enormous AI expenditures are creating enough value for investors.

“That is why I’m downgrading Alphabet to Hold,” Rotstein noted.

The decision follows a second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow, with Alphabet reporting a $9.1 billion shortfall in Q3. Capital expenditures reached $51.4 billion, exceeding the $42.3 billion generated from operating activities. Meanwhile, the company has raised billions of dollars through debt and equity offerings as it continues its costly infrastructure expansion.

This represents a significant departure from Alphabet’s historical approach, when profits from Search and other established operations could finance new investments while leaving substantial resources available for share repurchases.

To be clear, the company’s growth remains impressive. Third-quarter revenue climbed 25% to $127.6 billion, while Google Cloud sales more than doubled to $30.7 billion. Nevertheless, Rotstein is concerned about slowing advertising growth, potential pressure on future profitability, and the absence of clear evidence that the latest spending commitments will generate adequate returns.

He also sees limited valuation protection; at approximately 25 times adjusted earnings, Alphabet does not appear especially inexpensive compared with other tech giants, particularly given its complicated financing requirements.

For Rotstein, the company remains a formidable competitor in artificial intelligence, but its financial trajectory needs to improve before he would consider becoming bullish again.

What Does Wall Street Think About Nvidia and Alphabet Stocks?

So, what does Wall Street think? Analysts aren’t giving up on either AI giant. Nvidia has earned a Moderate Buy consensus rating, with 30 Buys, 13 Holds, and one Sell. Its average price target of $232.59 points to a potential gain of ~82%. Alphabet looks even more popular among analysts, with 30 Buys and just 4 Holds, giving it a Strong Buy consensus rating. However, its average target of $398.50 implies a smaller, though still attractive, 48% upside. (See NVDA stock forecast or GOOGL stock forecast)

data.title: AMD: Unfairly Maligned, or Right Where It Belongs?
data.description:
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell 7.7% on Thursday due to a negative report from Hunterbrook Media. Investors are asking, is this report credible?

What is Hunterbrook? There is Hunterbrook Media, which reported Thursday that products created by AMD are in the possession of backlisted companies in China.

There is also Hunterbrook Capital LP, a related hedge fund based in New York. That fund has opened a short position in AMD. Hunterbrook Capital is apparently hedging this trade with a long position in what it describes as “a basket of comparable securities.” 

Individuals can also hedge their investments, as explained here.

Best of the Bunch?

Despite Thursday’s selloff, AMD is holding up better than many names in the semiconductor sector. The stock is still up 118% year-to-date. Compare this to competitor Nvidia (NVDA), which is down 22.7% for the year.

After a huge bullish run, we closed half of our AMD position late last year. We reduced the position by half once again this past July. We exited the remainder of our AMD shares on November 6, as reported here. We currently have no position in AMD.

SEC Exemption

According to an April 2026 SEC filing, Hunterbrook Capital LP manages about $119 million across its funds. Because it has less than $150 million under management, it qualifies as an Exempt Reporting Advisor (ERA). An ERA is exempt from full SEC registration and can only advise private funds. 

The fact that Hunterbrook Capital LP is small may reduce its credibility in the eyes of some. Meanwhile, AMD has denied any wrongdoing.

Casting Doubt

Several new outlets cast doubt on the Hunterbrook report. CNBC’s Jon Fortt challenged the accuracy of the report, saying it “didn’t make sense.” 

After the close, the U.S. Commerce Department further muddied the waters, noting that as of May 2026, it approved the sale of 879,000 AI chips to buyers in China. As of this writing, AMD has not commented on the Commerce Department statement.

Past Performance

We know that past performance is not indicative of future results, but just the same, we wanted to explore some of Hunterbrook’s prior shorts.

Hunterbrook Capital announced a short position in UWM Holdings (UWMC), a wholesale mortgage lender, in April 2024 (point A). At the time, the stock was trading near $6.50. 

The stock subsequently rallied. A trader that shorted UWMC in April could have lost nearly 50% by late August (point B).

Hunterbrook Media claimed that UWM Holdings engaged in questionable business practices. Hunterbrook Capital hedged its short position in UWMC with a long position in Rocket Mortgage.

UWM Holdings trades near $1.13 today (point C), losing nearly 87% from its August 2024 peak. Hunterbrook’s allegations against UWM Holdings may not be responsible for that decline, as the mortgage sector has been battered by high interest rates.

Bloom Energy

Bloom Energy (BE) manufactures and installs solid oxide fuel cell systems, which are used to provide on-site power in data centers. 

In July of this year, Hunterbrook announced that it shorted the stock (point A), accusing Bloom of using third-party companies to obscure its supply chain. This was allegedly done to cover up the use of companies based in China as part of that supply chain. 

Bloom Energy responded by describing the accusations as false and misleading.

In less than one month, shares of Bloom Energy fell nearly 40% to the $160 area (point B). During that month, the S&P 500 rose slightly, so we can’t blame the market. Despite a subsequent rally, the stock fell back to that area and is currently trading near $170 (point C). 

In this case, it does seem that Hunterbrook’s report had an impact on the stock. However, Bloom Energy’s more recent decline could be attributed to a general rotation away from AI and data center stocks. 

Bottom Line

It’s never been conclusively proven that any of the allegations made by Hunterbrook are either true or false. That said, AMD will be a litmus test for Hunterbrook, defining our perception of that company. 

If the allegations are false, the stock should bounce back. Hunterbrook may have just created a buying opportunity for AMD bulls. If the stock recovers, shorts — including Hunterbrook Capital — will take a loss. 

However, even if that’s the case, AMD exists within a weak sector, which exists within a weak market. It might be the best of its group, but right now, that’s not good enough. We’re staying flat.

data.title: 3 Vanguard ETFs Paying High Yields for Monthly Passive Income
data.description:
As stocks continue to lose ground and tech shares bear much of the selling, earning money without having to rely on market rallies is becoming appealing. For investors looking to put their money to work while navigating Wall Street’s latest downturn, high-yield ETFs offer an attractive possibility: regular cash distributions, diversification, and the potential to build a steady stream of passive income.

Vanguard, one of the world’s largest investment managers, offers several ETFs designed to deliver attractive income through monthly distributions. Using the TipRanks Best Vanguard ETFs tool, we’ve pinpointed three worth considering: Vanguard High-Yield Active ETF (VGHY), Vanguard Emerging Markets Government Bond ETF (VWOB), and Vanguard Long-Term Corporate Bond ETF (VCLT). Together, they offer yields exceeding 6%, monthly income potential, and exposure to three distinct segments of the bond market.

Vanguard High-Yield Active ETF (VGHY)

The Vanguard High-Yield Active ETF (VGHY) takes a relatively simple approach to generating income. It lends money to companies willing to pay higher interest rates, then passes much of that income along to investors. The catch is that these aren’t necessarily Wall Street’s safest borrowers. VGHY focuses on high-yield corporate bonds, commonly known as junk bonds, where greater credit risk comes with the potential for bigger payouts. And rather than following an index, Vanguard’s portfolio managers actively decide which bonds are worth owning and which risks aren’t worth taking.

VGHY charges an annual expense ratio of just 0.22%, while offering a 6.28% dividend yield. Better yet for income seekers, distributions arrive monthly rather than quarterly. As of October 31, the fund held 605 securities and managed about $312.7 million in assets. Among its largest recently disclosed positions were bonds associated with TransDigm and Nissan Motor Acceptance, alongside U.S. Treasury securities. No single position accounted for even 1% of the portfolio, meaning the fund isn’t betting too heavily on any one borrower.

So, why might VGHY deserve a place in an income-focused portfolio? Consider someone investing $20,000. At a 6.28% annual yield, that translates into about $1,256 a year, or $105 per month, before taxes and assuming distributions remain unchanged. That’s money arriving without having to sell shares or wait for the stock market to recover. Of course, higher yields aren’t free money, and weaker borrowers can run into trouble when economic conditions deteriorate. Still, for investors comfortable taking on additional credit risk, VGHY offers a relatively inexpensive way to turn a diversified bond portfolio into a monthly income stream.

Vanguard Emerging Markets Government Bond ETF (VWOB)

The Vanguard Emerging Markets Government Bond ETF (VWOB) takes investors well beyond the U.S. bond market, putting their money to work in countries such as Argentina, Mexico, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia. Rather than lending primarily to companies, as VGHY does, this fund focuses on U.S. dollar-denominated bonds issued by emerging-market governments, government agencies, and state-owned enterprises. It’s a way to collect interest from borrowers around the world without having to buy foreign bonds individually. And unlike VGHY, which relies on active portfolio managers, VWOB follows the Bloomberg USD Emerging Markets Government RIC Capped Index.

VWOB also comes with an attractive price tag, charging an annual expense ratio of just 0.15%, compared with VGHY’s 0.22%. The fund offers a 6.20% dividend yield, with distributions paid monthly. Its portfolio contains more than 900 bond holdings, backed by ~$6.6 billion in total assets. Among its five largest individual positions are three Argentine government bonds and two bonds issued by Mexico’s state-owned oil company, Pemex.

Of course, lending money to emerging-market governments comes with risks, including political instability, sovereign defaults, and changing interest rates. But for investors willing to accept those uncertainties, VWOB offers an inexpensive way to earn monthly income from countries that might otherwise be difficult to access.

Vanguard Long-Term Corporate Bond ETF (VCLT)

The Vanguard Long-Term Corporate Bond ETF (VCLT) takes another route to generating income, focusing on established companies rather than riskier corporate borrowers or emerging-market governments. The fund tracks the Bloomberg U.S. 10+ Year Corporate Bond Index, investing in investment-grade corporate bonds with maturities exceeding 10 years. That means investors are lending money to some of the biggest names in corporate America for extended periods, collecting interest along the way. The trade-off is that longer-term bonds are particularly sensitive to interest rate movements, meaning their market values can fall considerably when borrowing costs rise.

VCLT also happens to be the cheapest of the three Vanguard ETFs, charging an annual expense ratio of just 0.03%. The fund is also considerably larger, managing about $9.5 billion across 2,647 holdings. Among its largest corporate bond positions are Anheuser-Busch, CVS Health, Boeing, Meta Platforms, and Pfizer. Meanwhile, investors receive monthly distributions backed by an attractive 6.00% dividend yield.

For investors who can tolerate the volatility that comes with long-duration bonds, VCLT offers a low-cost way to collect monthly income from established corporate borrowers.

data.title: Micron vs. Sandisk: One AI Stock Has the Edge, but Is It a Buy, Asks Investor
data.description:
Ouch. Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) picked a memorable day to start handing out seven new shares for every one its investors already owned. The stock’s first split-adjusted session landed in the middle of yet another rout in AI names, and memory makers like Sandisk and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) were among the hardest hit. A lower sticker price is little comfort when the whole sector is being marked down.

The selling started in Asia, where indexes in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan each fell more than 5%. At the time of writing, the Nasdaq 100 is down almost 4%, Micron has shed more than 12%, and Sandisk an even heavier 14%.

A day earlier, TrendForce said NAND flash contract prices should begin slipping in the first quarter of 2027 as Chinese cloud providers cut back on enterprise SSD orders.

With both stocks now down massively from their June highs, an investor using the pseudonym Delta Analyst (DA) set out to stress-test that scenario. Rather than debating whether NAND prices will fall, the investor asks how big a drop today’s share prices can already absorb, using through-cycle cash flow instead of earnings multiples.

A NAND slump would hit the two companies very differently. Sandisk is a pure flash play, and its fiscal first-quarter revenue soared 378% year over year, mostly on higher prices and a richer mix rather than more bits. That makes Sandisk the more exposed of the two. Its cushion is that prices have climbed so far that even halving them would leave them well above last year’s levels.

Micron leans on DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, where DA sees pricing on firmer ground, and it has guided fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue to $61.5 billion. Its weak spot is spending. Micron runs its own fabs and laid out $27.4 billion in net capex in fiscal 2026, so what matters is how much cash survives the next round of building. Sandisk buys its wafers through its Flash Ventures partnership with Kioxia, which keeps its spending light, though it still covers its share of the venture’s costs.

Both companies have locked in customers. Sandisk’s New Business Models deals with eight large buyers cover about half of its fiscal 2027 bits and two-thirds of fiscal 2028 bits, with remaining performance obligations of $88.9 billion, while Micron has its own Strategic Customer Agreements. DA warns that none of this is cash in hand. How much of a price drop Sandisk’s contracts would absorb is still unclear, though the investor suspects they may hold up better than spot prices suggest.

The supply picture is the main threat. TrendForce expects NAND bit supply to grow 25% to 30% in 2027. DA reads that as support for the idea that NAND prices will come back down toward more normal levels. Still, that’s an industry forecast. Much of Sandisk’s output is sold under long-term contracts, so its own prices may not fall as far or as fast as the market’s.

DA models Sandisk’s fiscal 2028 with 35% bit growth and a 15% drop in cost per bit. If blended prices fall 35%, normalized owner cash flow lands at about $17.5 billion, a 14.7% yield on its market cap. A 50% price drop cuts that yield to 9.1%. By DA’s math, the stock can absorb a cumulative price decline of roughly 35% and still deliver about 10% annual returns, but a steeper slide or bigger manufacturing bills could do serious damage.

Micron goes through the same test. DA’s central case has fiscal 2028 revenue of $250 billion at a 75% gross margin, with $50 billion in net capex, producing owner cash flow of about $88 billion, a 10.9% yield. That puts the value close to where the stock traded when the investor ran the numbers. In the bear case, with revenue at $200 billion and capex at $55 billion, the yield drops to 5%.

Putting it together, DA sees Micron’s DRAM and HBM mix as the more durable earnings base, even if its valuation leaves little room for higher spending or an early price drop. Sandisk carries more NAND risk, though its share price already reflects a good part of it. In the investor’s view, however, neither offers enough margin of safety to justify buying.

That leaves DA rating both Micron and Sandisk stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral), although if pushed, Delta Analyst has a preference for Micron. (To watch Delta Analyst’s track record, click here)

In contrast to DA, most Street analysts are bullish on both MU and SNDK, with the pair claiming Strong Buy consensus ratings. At $1,624, MU’s average price target offers 12-month upside of 169%. SNDK’s $2,003 average target (before the stock split) suggests shares will gain 165% in the year ahead. (See MU stock forecast or SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Nobody Knows,’ Says Investor on Anthropic Stock
data.description:
Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) got the welcome every company dreams of on its first day on the public markets. A day later, it is getting treated like every other AI stock this fall. The Claude maker priced its offering above the expected range on Wednesday, and buyers rushed in when it began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. By Friday morning, a wide tech selloff and renewed doubts about the AI trade were pulling shares lower.

The stock opened at $111.50 on Thursday, 34% above its $83 IPO price. It ended the session at $97.17, still a 17% gain. At the time of writing, it is down by 12% in Friday’s trading. That’s quite a welcome to the current volatile AI market.

Against this backdrop, investor Kenio Fontes has been taking a look at this hyped stock and doesn’t doubt that the business is the real thing.

Third-quarter revenue reached $17.0 billion, up 1,127% year over year. Net revenue retention is about 900%, which means existing customers are spending roughly nine times what they spent a year ago. More than 11,900 customers now pay $100,000 or more a year, compared with about 950 a year earlier. Fontes sees this as proof that a premium model provider can stand out in a market full of free and cheap options. He also thinks Claude could grow into a full enterprise platform, which would make customers harder to lose.

The trouble starts when he tries to put a value on all that. His generous long-term case has Anthropic reaching 30,000 large customers worldwide by 2036, with spending per customer compounding about 10% a year and an adjusted operating margin of 35% once the business matures. That gets him to about $176 billion in adjusted operating income. It’s a solid figure, but it already assumes strong execution, and investors would have to wait a decade for it.

He also works from the top down. Anthropic’s prospectus values global knowledge work at more than $40 trillion. After his own assumptions about adoption, productivity gains and the share AI providers can charge, Fontes ends up with about $100 billion in potential revenue for Anthropic. New Street Research, by contrast, expects revenue above $500 billion by 2030. To Fontes, that gap is the whole problem. The valuation can look fair if you believe the bigger numbers, but nobody knows how large the market will be or how much of it Anthropic will keep.

Competition worries him most. With OpenAI, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta all in the race, he doubts Anthropic can hold even a 20% to 30% share for the long run. Stock-based compensation is another concern. The adjusted figures leave it out, and under GAAP accounting Anthropic posted a $1.26 billion operating loss over the first nine months of 2026.

Fontes notes that the IPO cash gives Anthropic a clean balance sheet and makes near-term borrowing or dilution less likely. But he sees no margin of safety at this price. He would rather keep his exposure to Anthropic through his holdings in Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia.

That leaves Fontes with a Sell rating on Anthropic stock. (To watch Fontes’s track record, click here)

However, none of the Street’s analysts are on the same page here. So far, based on 6 Buys vs. 1 Hold, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $133.33 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for a 57% premium. (See ANT stock forecast)

data.description:
Investors looking to reduce portfolio volatility may consider low-beta ETFs. These funds tend to move less than the broader stock market, which may help limit price swings during market ups and downs. Using TipRanks’ Best Vanguard ETFs tool, three relatively safer options stand out: Vanguard Mortgage-Backed Securities ETF (VMBS), Vanguard Total Treasury ETF (VTG), and Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC).

Today, technology and AI stocks remained under pressure after Thursday’s steep selloff. Anthropic (ANT) stock fell 11.1% after it gained 17% on its first trading day yesterday. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, selling 980 million shares at $83 each.

Vanguard Mortgage-Backed Securities ETF (VMBS)

The Vanguard Mortgage-Backed Securities ETF invests in U.S. government-backed mortgage bonds. It tracks the performance of the Bloomberg U.S. MBS Float Adjusted Index.

VMBS has a very low beta of 0.0, meaning its price tends to show little correlation with broader stock market movements. This may make it useful for investors looking to reduce overall portfolio volatility. VMBS also has a low expense ratio of about 0.03%.

The ETF has a dividend yield of 4.36%.

Vanguard Total Treasury ETF (VTG)

The Vanguard Total Treasury ETF gives investors exposure to U.S. government bonds. It invests in a mix of Treasury bills, notes, and bonds across different time periods. Since these bonds are backed by the U.S. government, VTG is considered a very safe investment.

VTG has a beta of 0.01. It tends to remain stable even when stock markets fluctuate, making it a suitable option for investors seeking stability.

VTG has a dividend yield of 3.90% and an expense ratio of 0.03%.

Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC)

The Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF focuses on companies that sell everyday essential products such as food, beverages, and household goods. These businesses tend to be more stable because demand for their products stays relatively steady even during economic slowdowns. VDC holds 105 stocks with total assets worth $8.42 billion.

However, its growth potential is usually more limited, since consumer staples companies typically expand at a slower, steadier pace.

VDC has a beta of 0.23, which means it is much less volatile than the overall market. It has a slightly higher expense ratio than the other two ETFs at 0.09%. The ETF has a dividend yield of 1.99%.

data.title: Down Nearly 50%, Is Micron Stock Ripe for the Picking? Investor Weighs In
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) keeps telling Wall Street that next year will be its best ever, and its shares keep heading the other way. Today represents another bloodbath, with Anthropic giving back a chunk of its first-day gains and dragging the AI trade lower with it. Micron, which bought into Anthropic’s IPO, is among the hardest-hit chip stocks.

Yesterday, research firm TrendForce warned that NAND flash contract prices should start slipping in early 2027 as Chinese cloud providers pull back on enterprise SSD orders. Yet the selling comes after Micron said at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin on Wednesday that it expects memory supply in 2027 and 2028 to be tighter than in 2026. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said 75% of Micron’s 2027 supply is already sold out, with customer talks now moving on to 2028. Micron shares are down about 10% on Friday, leaving the stock nearly 50% below its late-June record close.

Watching the slide, investor Cain Lee doesn’t think it says much about Micron’s business. As the investor sees it, 2027 isn’t really in doubt. The concern sits further out, at the point when all the extra capacity being built by Micron, Sandisk and SK hynix comes online. Lee thinks the market has jumped ahead to price in a 2028 downturn and has gone too far.

The latest numbers support that view. In its fiscal fourth quarter, reported Sept. 30, Micron’s revenue climbed 379% year over year to $54.2 billion, and adjusted EPS of $33.42 topped estimates. Management expects revenue to grow every quarter of fiscal 2027. It also expects the current quarter, with gross margin guided at about 86%, to be the year’s low point for margins.

What stands out most to Lee is how much of the future is already locked in. Micron now has 26 strategic customer agreements, which it expects to cover more than 35% of revenue through 2030. Customers have put up $32 billion in commitments, mostly deposits, and remaining performance obligations total about $150 billion. That figure is calculated at minimum contract prices, which Lee considers a cautious way to count it. Pricing is still moving in Micron’s favor, too, with TrendForce expecting conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% this quarter. With the stock at about 4x forward earnings, the investor sees plenty of bad news already priced in.

Of course, that’s not to say the risks should be completely ignored. Micron isn’t the only one building, so a lot of new supply could land at once, and the company itself raised its fiscal 2027 capex plans. The contracts cover only about a third of revenue, and everything else is exposed to market prices. Taiwan accounts for about 60% of Micron’s DRAM output. There, a pay dispute led Micron to pause construction of a new fab in Taoyuan, according to reports, and talks with the local union are now in government-led mediation, with the next session set for Nov. 26. The investor worries the trouble could reach the plants already running.

Still, Lee points out that the AI buildout hasn’t slowed. Nvidia’s revenue more than doubled year over year last quarter, and big cloud spenders have signaled more spending ahead. With record results, higher guidance and a growing contract book, Lee thinks it’s time to pounce. “The pullback offers an opportunity in my opinion and the cheap valuation justifies accumulation here as the selloff becomes overdone,” Lee summed up, upgrading Micron stock from a Buy to a Strong Buy. (To watch Lee’s track record, click here)

That is also the conclusion reached by the analyst consensus, a rating based on 28 Buys and 1 Hold. At $1,624, the average price target implies shares will gain 163% over the one-year timeframe. (See MU stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Show Me the Proof,’ Says Investor About AMD Stock
data.description:
Often playing second fiddle, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) has been the chipmaker big AI customers turn to when they want something other than Nvidia, and the stock recently got a boost following the Jensen Huang saga.

On Thursday, a short seller argued that the picture is messier than it looks. Hunterbrook Media published reports alleging that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker on the U.S. blacklist, kept getting newer AMD firmware. The reports also questioned how much AMD spends to support its own customers. Hunterbrook’s sister fund, Hunterbrook Capital, disclosed a short position.

AMD said the claims misrepresent its business practices and relationships, and Hunterbrook itself says its findings don’t establish that AMD broke export law. The stock still closed down almost 8% on Thursday and is taking another heavy beating today, as the AI selloff that came with Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut carries on.

So, what are investors meant to do with all that information?

Investor Mike Zaccardi, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, read the same reports and isn’t rattled. He says Hunterbrook hasn’t shown any wrongdoing, and until someone does, the allegations are guesswork.

What he does see is a business whose main engine is running hot. In the third quarter, reported on Nov. 3, revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. Data Center sales nearly doubled to $8.5 billion on demand for EPYC server processors, the launch of the Instinct MI450 GPUs and the first customers taking Helios rack-scale systems. Embedded revenue grew 29% to $1.1 billion, more than making up for an 8% drop in Client and Gaming to $3.7 billion. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion and a non-GAAP gross margin of roughly 55%. The investor thinks margins can hold even as HBM gets more expensive. He also sees room for AMD to win business while Nvidia deals with the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO on Nov. 12.

On valuation, Zaccardi looks past the current growth spurt to 2028, where he assumes about $23 in normalized EPS. As long as gross margins stay high, he believes AMD deserves a premium multiple. For context, the stock trades at around 30x the consensus 2027 EPS estimate of roughly $16.

The 5-star investor doesn’t play down the risks involved here. Competition in AI accelerators and custom chips is fierce, and pricier memory and parts could eat into margins. Export-control scrutiny matters more now that data centers bring in a bigger share of sales. Customer warrants, including ones that let OpenAI and Meta buy up to 160 million shares each, could dilute existing holders. The chart is weak too, and Zaccardi expects the shares to trade sideways for a while rather than bounce straight back.

Even so, he thinks the earnings growth and resilient margins count for more than a short thesis nobody has backed up yet, and that the drop gives patient buyers a better way in.

All told, Zaccardi rates AMD a Buy. (To watch Zaccardi’s track record, click here)

So do the majority of Street stock experts. The analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy, based on 29 Buys vs. 3 Holds. At $652.18, the average price target offers 12-month upside of 48%. (See AMD stock forecast)

data.title: Disney (DIS) Is Catching Up to Netflix (NFLX), but the Upside May Be Shrinking
data.description:
The Walt Disney Company (DIS) is catching up to Netflix (NFLX) in valuation, leaving less upside for its stock even as its streaming business gains ground.

The California-based entertainment giant’s fiscal fourth-quarter results, released on November 17, showed that the company’s recovery is gaining momentum. Operating profit for Disney+ and Hulu more than doubled to $824 million, while the Experiences segment posted a 20% increase in operating profit to $2.25 billion.

What’s interesting is that this operational rebound comes just as Netflix is losing much of the valuation premium it has carried for years. Today, both stocks trade at virtually identical forward earnings multiples near 16x, despite very different business models — a pure-play streamer versus a capital-heavy media and parks conglomerate.

In my view, Disney’s turnaround is convincing, but the stock’s risk-reward no longer looks that attractive. I prefer Netflix at current valuations and maintain a Hold rating on DIS.

Disney and Netflix Are Closing the Valuation Gap

We may be entering a new chapter in the streaming wars, with Disney and Netflix closing the valuation gap. For years, Netflix was the clear winner on Wall Street, commanding a hefty valuation premium. Over the past five years, it traded at an average of 38.6x non-GAAP earnings. Meanwhile, Disney struggled to convince investors that its streaming ambitions would pay off, trading at an average of just 25.8x non-GAAP earnings over the same period. That’s despite Disney having a much broader business beyond streaming.

Now the tables seem to be turning. Both companies trade at roughly 16x forward earnings, with enterprise values hovering around $250 billion. Interestingly, they’ve arrived at this point from opposite directions. Netflix shares have fallen nearly 45% over the past year, while Disney has gained around 19%. In other words, Disney isn’t just catching up. Netflix is also losing some of its valuation premium.

Of course, Disney’s streaming business, reported as Subscription Video on Demand (SVOD), has played an increasingly important role in this shift. Although Disney+ and Hulu account for just 22% of the company’s revenue, they contributed nearly 60% of its total segment operating profit growth in Fiscal 2026. Streaming profits nearly doubled to $2.57 billion, making the business a key driver of Disney’s earnings growth.

Disney’s Streaming Profits Are Finally Catching Up

As Disney reported its Q4 results, I would argue that the most interesting part was how quickly streaming profits were growing.

For example, Disney+ and Hulu generated $6.05 billion in revenue, up 19% year-over-year, while operating income more than doubled to $824 million. Even excluding the estimated $160 million benefit from an extra accounting week, streaming profits grew roughly 65%. The quarterly operating margin reached 13.6%, compared with 11.5% for Fiscal 2026 as a whole. These are impressive improvements for a business that, not too long ago, was still losing billions of dollars annually.

More importantly, they suggest that Disney is finally starting to enjoy the kind of operating leverage that made Netflix such a profitable business in the first place.

Even so, Disney has a long way to go before matching Netflix’s profitability. Netflix reported a 34.6% operating margin in Q3 and expects 31.5% for the full year.

Yet that’s also where I see the opportunity. With Disney generating roughly $22.3 billion in annual streaming revenue, every five percentage points of additional operating margin could add more than $1.1 billion in annual operating profit, even without further revenue growth.

The caveat is that, starting next quarter (Fiscal 2027), Disney will no longer report streaming operating income separately. That will make this significant growth driver harder for investors to track.

Disney Has More Than Netflix, but at What Cost?

Of course, Disney isn’t just another Netflix. It’s actually much more than that. That’s not necessarily a good thing. In fact, it’s one reason why the two companies shouldn’t necessarily trade at the same valuation.

While streaming accounts for just 13% of Disney’s total segment operating profit, Experiences, which includes parks and cruises, remains the real earnings powerhouse. The segment generated $11.2 billion in operating profit in Fiscal 2026, or roughly 57% of the total. The other arm, Sports, which includes ESPN, contributed another $3.1 billion.

What’s particularly interesting is how Disney can monetize the same intellectual property across movies, streaming, theme parks, cruises, and merchandise. Netflix has been expanding beyond streaming too, but Disney’s ecosystem is much more established. The latest Fiscal Q4 earnings reinforced the strength of this model. Experiences revenue rose 15%, while operating income grew 20%. Sports operating profit also jumped 53%.

The problem is that maintaining this entire ecosystem makes Disney highly cash-intensive. Disney expects $9 billion in capital expenditures and around $26 billion in content spending in Fiscal 2027. That’s a reminder that Disney’s diversified model may offer more ways to grow, but not necessarily the same capital efficiency as Netflix.

This is already reflected in cash flow. Disney generated $10.6 billion in free cash flow in Fiscal 2026 and expects just $11 billion in Fiscal 2027, implying growth of only about 4%. So, much of the earnings improvement has yet to translate into meaningful cash flow growth.

Netflix, meanwhile, expects around $12 billion in free cash flow this year, although that includes a one-time $2.8 billion termination fee. Even excluding this windfall, Netflix’s free cash flow margin would be roughly 18%, compared with Disney’s 11%.

Wall Street Loves Disney, but Sees More Upside in Netflix

Based on Wall Street sentiment, it’s easy to see why Disney remains a favorite. All 16 analysts covering DIS over the past three months recommend buying the stock, giving it a Strong Buy consensus.

However, there’s an interesting contradiction. Disney’s average price target of $136.25 implies just 13.3% upside, while Netflix’s $85 target suggests over 45.4%, despite its less enthusiastic Moderate Buy consensus.

To me, this reflects two very different investment opportunities. Disney offers greater earnings visibility, supported by improving streaming profitability and resilient parks. Netflix, meanwhile, faces slowing growth and more uncertainty. Yet its nearly 45% sell-off may have created a more attractive entry point.

That’s why I’m not particularly bullish on DIS at current levels. I like the direction of its business, but the stock’s upside looks relatively limited. For now, I prefer Netflix’s risk-reward and would rather stay on the sidelines with Disney.

Disney Is Winning the Streaming Battle, but Not the Valuation War

Disney is clearly in a much better position than it was a few years ago. Streaming is finally delivering meaningful profits, while its broader entertainment business continues to show resilience.

The next challenge is turning these improvements into stronger free cash flow growth, especially as Disney continues to invest heavily across its businesses.

With Netflix now trading at a similar earnings multiple, I see a more compelling opportunity there. Until Disney shows more progress on cash flow, I believe a Hold rating makes the most sense.

data.title: Nvidia vs. Alphabet: One AI Stock Is Trouble, the Other Offers Opportunity, Says Investor
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) earns its living when companies like Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) pour money into AI, and this fall investors have found reasons to worry about both sides of that arrangement. Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday beat expectations and lifted the outlook. The shares kept sliding anyway, as investors weigh Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO last week and how the AI buildout is being paid for. Alphabet’s third-quarter report on Oct. 28 showed its cloud unit growing faster than ever, but the cost of keeping up has left shareholders uneasy.

Both stocks are a long way from their peaks. Nvidia is sitting at a 52-week low, nearly 40% below its early-October record close. Alphabet is about 32% under its May 13 record close of $402.62.

With both stocks at depressed levels, opportunity could be opening up for investors here. However, investor Nicolas Bolsinger has studied both and lands in different places on them.

He has no quarrel with Nvidia’s latest numbers. Revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion, and management guided to about $130 billion for the current quarter. What worries the investor is how much of that demand Nvidia now helps fund. The company carries up to $118 billion in guarantees tied to AI infrastructure, roughly a third of its sales over the past four quarters. Of that, $105 billion is linked to a single Ohio campus that SB Energy is leasing to OpenAI. Bolsinger also counts about $110 billion in stakes in other companies, including SpaceX and CoreWeave.

He compares this to Nortel, the telecom-gear maker that lent heavily to its own customers around 2000. By his math, Nortel’s financing was smaller relative to its sales than Nvidia’s guarantees are now. Nortel kept promising solid growth until its revenue fell by more than a third. In a spending boom, he argues, upbeat guidance is usually the last thing to change.

The debt market adds to his unease. CoreWeave, one of the companies Nvidia has invested in, carries a B+ credit rating from S&P and a Ba3 from Moody’s. Yet by Bolsinger’s math, its bonds were yielding about 13.5% at the end of September, much closer to what the riskiest tier of junk borrowers pays. To him, that means bond investors see Nvidia’s partners as shakier than the rating agencies do.

The Federal Reserve’s Nov. 13 Financial Stability Report flagged “circular financing” in the data center buildout. Fed Governor Michael Barr later put the potential maximum value of the related obligations above $3 trillion. The Fed took comfort in the idea that large firms could absorb losses in a downturn. Bolsinger sees that as the problem, because Nvidia is one of those firms.

He also flags a gross margin guide of 71% to 72%, down from 74.9%. He isn’t impressed by a forward P/E at multi-year lows either, since a cyclical stock tends to look cheapest when profits peak.

Nvidia’s strong balance sheet is the only thing keeping him from a Strong Sell, and he rates the stock a Sell on a 12-month view. (To watch Bolsinger’s track record, click here)

Alphabet looks almost like the mirror image to the investor. Revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, Google Cloud sales jumped 103% YoY to $30.7 billion, and the CFO put Cloud’s backlog at $561 billion.

The trouble is paying for it. Capital spending has outpaced operating cash flow for two straight quarters, leaving free cash flow at negative $9.1 billion in Q3. Buybacks are on hold, and long-term debt has reached $125.1 billion. In June, Alphabet unveiled an equity raise of about $85 billion, including $10 billion from Berkshire Hathaway. Bolsinger thinks the market is punishing the share sales more than the cash burn itself. He points to Amazon, which has burned more cash without selling stock and has held up better.

A trailing P/E of about 14 makes Alphabet look cheaper than it is, since its profits have been padded by paper gains on private stakes such as SpaceX. Bolsinger strips those out, and on his math the stock trades around the middle of its five-year range. What has changed is the business, which is growing at its fastest pace since 2021. In his view, investors are paying a typical price for a much stronger company.

That’s where he sees the upside. The stock is being held back by worries over how Alphabet pays for its AI spending, and he thinks that’s a problem it can fix. Microsoft, which pays its way from its own cash, doesn’t have a problem like that to solve, so it has no comparable boost waiting.

Alphabet does, and Bolsinger expects that fix to come from slowing the growth in its spending. That would restore cash flow and leave chip suppliers with less pricing power, which is the other half of his Nvidia view. He would turn more cautious if capex keeps climbing while free cash flow worsens, or if Alphabet launches another large stock sale.

With the business this strong and the fix in its own hands, he rates Alphabet a Buy.

On the Street, Nvidia claims a Moderate Buy consensus view, while its $232.59 average price target implies shares will gain 59% in the months ahead. GOOGL is rated a Strong Buy. The stock is expected to appreciate by 46%, given the average target clocks in at $398.50. (See Nvidia stock forecast or Alphabet stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Bad Timing?’ Big-Money Investors Loaded Up on Nvidia Stock Just Before It Cracked
data.description:
Quarterly 13F filings always arrive late, and this round makes for uncomfortable reading on Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). The reports show what the big funds owned at the end of September, when the chipmaker was only days away from a record high. A lot has happened since. Investors began to question how the AI buildout is being paid for, and then Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12. A strong fiscal third-quarter report on Tuesday did little to stop the slide.

Now the shares sit about 40% below their Oct. 6 record close of $239.24 and more than a third below where they ended September. So any fund that bought during the quarter and held on is now looking at a paper loss on those shares.

There were plenty of buyers. Tiger Global raised its stake by 7% to 12 million shares, making Nvidia its largest holding. Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter Capital, a holder since late 2022, went to about 10 million shares from 9.4 million. David Tepper’s Appaloosa added 475,000 shares, a 31% increase, for a 2 million-share position worth about $457 million on Sept. 30. Dan Loeb’s Third Point opened a new stake of 1.5 million shares valued at roughly $343 million, along with new bets on Meta and Microsoft.

Others were heading for the exit. Bridgewater Associates cut its position by about 30% to roughly 2.7 million shares. Soros Fund Management sold about 206,000 shares, a 19% trim that left it with around 859,000. Renaissance Technologies sold more than 99% of a stake that had stood at about 7.1 million shares in June. Fidelity’s parent, FMR, reduced its holding by 9%, though Nvidia is still its largest reported position.

Duan Yongping’s H&H International cut its stake by about 63%, but that number may overstate how much he actually sold. Duan often uses options to manage his positions, and 13Fs only list stock, so part of the drop could come from options being exercised rather than outright selling. He also said this week that most of his reasons for owning Nvidia still hold, and that he is in no hurry to sell.

By HedgeFollow’s count, more funds were buying than selling, with 592 hedge funds adding Nvidia shares in the quarter against 465 that sold. But a 13F only shows what a fund held on one day, Sept. 30. It says nothing about what managers did once the selling began in October. Renaissance is also a quant fund that trades on model signals rather than a view of Nvidia’s leadership, so its exit can’t be read as a call on a scandal that broke weeks later.

Wall Street, for its part, is mostly still on board. Analysts give NVDA a Moderate Buy consensus rating, based on 30 Buys, 13 Holds and 1 Sell. The average price target of $232.59 implies shares will rise by 59% in the months ahead. (See NVDA stock forecast)

SpaceX Delivers a Strong Q3

SpaceX reported Q3 revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161% year-over-year. Net profit reached $4.4 billion, well above the $1.8 billion forecast. AI revenue rose more than ninefold to $7.6 billion, while connectivity revenue, which includes Starlink, grew 69% to $5.25 billion.

CFO Bret Johnsen also said Q1 2027 revenue could reach $33 billion to $37 billion. That is well above the $22.2 billion analyst estimate.

Latest Analysts’ Views on SPCX

Bernstein analyst Douglas Harned kept a Buy rating on SPCX stock with a price target of $268. This points to more than 90% upside.

Harned believes the current shortage of AI computing power gives SpaceX a chance to earn back its investment fast. Elon Musk aims to add at least 20 gigawatts (GW) of power and 10GW of computing capacity by the end of 2027. SpaceX expects to have about 3GW of computing capacity by the end of 2026. The analyst expects SpaceX to charge close to $50 per watt in the first half of 2027. He said that at this price, “it can monetize the investment in less than 12 months.”

Morgan Stanley’s analyst Adam Jonas also kept his Buy rating and $300 price target on SpaceX. He called SPCX the “ultimate off-the-grid” stock because its Starlink network does not rely on the ground-based systems behind recent outages at Microsoft (MSFT) Outlook, the FAA, and the NSA. Jonas said rising demand for backup systems could help space-based internet services.

He further pointed to Starlink’s steady revenue model and plans for about $490 billion in Terafab spending through 2035. The analyst also noted that SpaceX’s 2028 earnings multiple is below that of the S&P 500.

Anthropic Q3 Revenue Soars 1,127%

Ahead of its IPO, Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $17 billion, up 1,127% from the same period in 2025. The company reported revenue of $33.24 billion for the nine months of 2026, up 1,200% from the same period a year ago. But Anthropic’s revenue growth slowed from one quarter to the next. Revenue rose 47% in the third quarter, down from 144% growth in the second quarter and 132% in the first quarter.

Anthropic is also still losing money. The company reported a net loss of $104 billion through September, more than four times its $25.1 billion loss in the same period last year. In the third quarter alone, its net loss reached $23.29 billion.

Wall Street’s Views on ANT Stock

Citizens’ analyst Patrick Walravens has started coverage of Anthropic (ANT) with a Buy rating and a $125 price target. He noted that Anthropic has a strong team, with all seven co-founders still at the company nearly six years after it was set up. Walravens also sees Anthropic’s approach to computing as a key strength. The company trains and runs its Claude AI model across four major chip types, giving it more ways to use computing power.

William Blair’s analyst Arjun Bhatia also started coverage of Anthropic with a Buy rating. Bhatia expects the AI market to reach at least $5 trillion. He also forecasts that Anthropic’s revenue could hit $414 billion by 2030. He values the company at 9 times its expected 2027 revenue and 6 times its 2028 revenue. Based on a 17-20 times revenue multiple, he sees Anthropic’s fair value at $130 to $150 per share.

SPCX or ANT: Which Stock Offers Higher Upside, According to Analysts?

SpaceX has an average 12-month price target of $263.83, implying 90% upside. SPCX stock has 28 Buys, six Holds, and one Sell assigned in the last three months.

ANT stock has six Buys and one Hold. In comparison, Anthropic’s average price target of $133.33 suggests 37% upside.

data.title: Marvell Stock’s (MRVL) Plunge Is My Opportunity to Buy
data.description:
Marvell Technology (MRVL) stock has taken a mighty plunge, and I see the sell-off as my opportunity to buy. At $138.47, the shares are about 56% below their record close, weighed down by broader chip-sector weakness, fears of slowing artificial intelligence (AI) spending, and dilution concerns around its pending Lumentum (LITE) acquisition. While those risks are real, I think the market has overreacted, leaving a key supplier of custom AI chips and optical data-center links trading at a steep discount just as its Lumentum deal prepares to widen its competitive moat. That risk-reward balance makes MRVL a Buy for me.

I’m selective about AI stocks right now, given how much depends on big cloud providers’ spending and how sharply that growth could slow. Still, after the recent downturn in chip stocks, I like the price I’m paying for Marvell’s growth.

When Prices Fall, I Get Excited and Buy

As a value-conscious investor, I get excited when prices fall. As Warren Buffett taught, it pays to be greedy when others are fearful.

Right now, I think we may be looking at a bottom in MRVL, with a base forming around $132 to $145 per share. The stock traded as low as $132.54 on the first Thursday in November. I managed to buy around $137, and the opportunity doesn’t look like it’s over. MRVL still trades well below its 200-day moving average, with strong forecasted fundamental growth that could carry shares to new highs before long.

What I’m Paying for Marvell’s Growth

At $138.47, I’m paying just under 20x what analysts expect Marvell to earn per share in Fiscal 2028. On November 18, the shares traded at 13.34x trailing sales, close to their five-year average of 13.55x. What excites me about that valuation is how fast earnings could grow.

Wall Street’s estimates imply about 62% annualized growth in earnings per share (EPS) from Fiscal 2028 to Fiscal 2030. Marvell’s data center revenue grew 46% year-over-year in its fiscal second quarter. While the market has sold the stock down over near-term deal dilution and AI spending concerns, I think it’s a mistake to assume strong growth won’t materialize. The recent correction gives investors a healthy margin of safety even if earnings come in somewhat below consensus.

Marvell’s Lumentum Deal Could Widen Its Moat

Part of what gives me confidence in that multi-year earnings trajectory, and helps explain why the market has been nervous, is Marvell’s pending deal for Lumentum. The deal would bring the lasers that send data through fiber-optic cables in-house. Marvell will issue new shares to pay for the deal, which the companies expect to close in the first half of 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

Management sees more than a billion dollars in potential annual cost savings, mainly through supply-chain scale, overlapping product lines, and shared research and overhead. Even with more shares outstanding, it expects Marvell to earn more adjusted profit per share in the first year after closing than it would on its own.

The risk is that Marvell ends up with more shares splitting too little profit. Lumentum’s two largest end customers accounted for 48% of its sales in the quarter ended September 2026. If either delays orders, Lumentum’s factories still cost money to run. It would be a mistake to view this as a risk-free deal, but I think the medium-term structural upside potential far outweighs near-term sentiment concerns.

The AI Buildout Isn’t Over Yet

Perhaps most important to my MRVL thesis is that I don’t think the AI buildout is anywhere near over. I’m looking beyond the next 12 months to 2028 to judge how durable Marvell’s upside could be once spending growth slows.

Morgan Stanley (MS) expects major cloud and infrastructure companies to spend around $1.77 trillion on capital projects in 2028. That would take annual spending growth from roughly 75% in 2027 to about 7% in 2028. Some providers may even cut spending. At that pace, investors may pay less for each dollar of chipmakers’ earnings.

I think Marvell could continue to appreciate even if Nvidia (NVDA) trades sideways for a while. Moving data between chips takes power, and Marvell’s optical links can move more data per watt. That gives cloud providers a reason to keep buying even if they delay the next data center. If the facilities they’re already building fill up and generate more cash, I think spending growth could pick up again.

What Does Wall Street Think of MRVL Stock?

Wall Street rates MRVL a Strong Buy, based on 24 Buys, five Holds, and no Sells. The average 12-month analyst price target is $323.63, which implies 133.72% upside. That supports my own bullish view as a shareholder.

I’m Staying Bullish on MRVL

I’m staying bullish on MRVL after a correction I think was both healthy and due. We may see a spending cut or two, but cloud providers still have good reason to buy chips that make the data centers they’re already building cheaper to run. At this price, Marvell has the growth potential and operating quality I like. I’m holding my shares.

If the price drops below the recent low at $132.50, then I may have to watch my position more closely. However, as it stands, the medium-term fundamentals look resilient enough, and Marvell’s operations have the quality to make this a likely winning trade.

data.title: AI Investing Is Getting Riskier, but Meta and Amazon Stocks Could Come Out Ahead, Says UBS
data.description:
Wall Street is facing another turbulent period, with the scandal surrounding Nvidia adding to concerns about the outlook for AI. While the chip giant’s leadership troubles have weighed on investor sentiment, broader worries about the enormous spending required to support AI development have also contributed to market uncertainty.

Much of that concern revolves around the infrastructure needed to sustain AI growth. Data centers, advanced servers, cooling systems, and electricity supplies all require extensive investment, raising doubts about whether future revenues will justify the costs. Nevertheless, demand for computing capacity remains strong, suggesting that spending on AI infrastructure could continue growing over the coming years.

Despite these risks, UBS Chief Investment Officer Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi remains positive about the market’s prospects heading into 2027, with AI playing a central role in her outlook. In a recent note, Hoffmann-Burchardi explains why the bank expects investment to continue expanding, while warning that not every company will benefit equally.

“AI investment is accelerating, but so are the risks. We expect global AI-related investment to rise from USD 1.0 trillion in 2026 to USD 1.5 trillion in 2028, supported by constrained computing capacity and strong demand. Yet, cumulative US technology investment could approach USD 5.0 trillion by then. Revenues will probably have to reach at least USD 1.5 trillion by 2030 for the industry to earn an adequate return, and while this is possible, not every company may reap the rewards. Competition, price cuts, costly monetization, and open-weight models may threaten returns. External financing is also becoming harder, while market concentration, regulatory risks, and company-specific risks could increase volatility,” Hoffmann-Burchardi wrote.

Against this backdrop, established tech giants may be better positioned to navigate rising costs and growing competition. UBS analyst Karl Keirstead, who ranks among the top 3% of Wall Street analysts, has selected two familiar tech stocks that he believes offer solid upside potential through the end of 2027.

Adding to their appeal, both companies carry a Strong Buy consensus rating from the broader analyst community, according to the TipRanks database. Let’s take a closer look.

Meta Platforms (META)

We’ll start with Meta Platforms, the $1.58 trillion leader in the world’s social media field. The company is best known as the parent of Facebook, and its family of social media apps includes Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads. Together, these apps give Meta a huge reach, with the company reporting 3.64 billion daily active people across its family of apps in September 2026, up 3% from the previous year.

That reach is Meta’s greatest single advantage, as the company works to better fit its approach to today’s AI-centered world. The key to this change is the development of Muse, launched this past September. Muse is a new step in personal AI technology; rather than simply answering queries, Muse is a personal AI agent, capable of autonomously running multi-step background tasks on the user’s behalf.

Agentic AI is bursting with potential, and Meta created Muse to make use of that potential on a personal level. The AI can monitor online shopping prices or audit your subscription services to find the best deals; it can manage your emails and calendars, or even book a restaurant reservation. A small business version brings these services into the business world to manage work-related social media, or seek out new customers.

Meta’s AI forays also include the Llama family of open-source large language models, and the consumer-oriented Meta AI assistant. The company is also a leader in the VR headset field, and is developing AI-powered smart glasses. All of this takes money, however, and that brings us back to the core social media business.

Meta makes its money through selling targeted advertising space and access across its family of social apps. Meta’s ability to reach billions of people gives the company huge leverage with digital advertisers, and it shows in its earnings. In its last quarterly report, from 3Q26, Meta showed a revenue figure of $64.6 billion. This was up 26% year-over-year, and it beat the forecast by $1.2 billion. At the bottom line, Meta reported adjusted EPS of $7.40, excluding a $9.89 billion litigation charge related to a multistate legal settlement. This compared with reported GAAP earnings of $3.83 per share.

However, Meta’s heavy expenditure on expanding its AI capabilities and products comes at a price, visible in the cash flows. The cash flow from operating activities in Q3 was a solid $32.79 billion – but the free cash flow in the quarter was reported as a negative $2.12 billion.

This combination of a sound revenue foundation with high expenditures forms the core of Karl Keirstead’s thesis on Meta. In his coverage for UBS, he writes of this social media giant, “Positive investor sentiment about the prospect of Muse and Meta Business Agents may be enough to offset concerns about capex build, negative FCF and financing needs. In our view the stock at 20x 2027 GAAP EPS seems attractively priced given the recent momentum in its AI model and apps (not just infra) story. Meta is now a very different business and stock than even 18 months ago, when the company began a hard re-boot of its AI roadmap. The CEO as well as key MSL leaders are building a new ‘AI maximalist version of Meta’ and as we begin coverage of Meta shares, we will be almost singularly focused on this aspect of the story – training Muse AI models, the launch of the Muse personal agent and the push into associated business or enterprise use cases and the scaling and cost of the required compute infrastructure, benefiting from our coverage of Microsoft Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle and CoreWeave. We’ll ramp on the core Meta over time, but near-term, the AI story is driving the stock narrative.”

Keirstead is positive on the stock, in the end, and gives META shares a Buy rating and an $815 price target that implies a one-year upside potential of 32%. (To watch Keirstead’s track record, click here)

Like most of Wall Street’s tech mega-caps, Meta has picked up a lot of analyst reviews, 43 on file right now. These split into 37 Buys and 6 Holds, giving the stock its Strong Buy consensus rating. META is currently priced at $616.38, and its average price target of $857.24 suggests that it will gain 39% by this time next year. (See META stock forecast)

Amazon (AMZN)

The UBS pick we’ll look at is Amazon, another of Wall Street’s trillion-dollar-plus giants. Amazon is a dot-com survivor, and has built itself up into the world’s largest online retailer, and in fact, its only true peer in the ‘retail giant’ space is Walmart.

But where Walmart is primarily a retailer, Amazon has expanded into several other industries, with its North America and International segments accounting for about 82% of total revenue in 2025. While its online retail segment will never go away, and will provide a large-scale revenue stream, Amazon is working steadily to increase its non-retail footprint – and AI is central to that plan.

At the center of Amazon’s non-retail expansion is AWS, the company’s cloud computing platform, which provides infrastructure, storage, AI tools, and other services to customers worldwide. AWS is among the fastest-growing of Amazon’s various businesses, and has shown rapid expansion in recent years – the Q3 report showed that AWS generated $46 billion in revenue, for a 39% year-over-year gain, far higher than the 5% to 6% growth recorded by Amazon’s International and North America segments. AWS is known for its wide-ranging set of cloud-based tools and apps, and in recent years Amazon has been adding AI to that mix.

Amazon is also involved in the ‘back end’ of AI. The company has entered the AI-capable silicon chip business, with its Trainium semiconductor. This is an in-house custom-built AI accelerator family, and it has attracted attention from some of the AI model providers. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has committed to using up to 5 gigawatts of AWS Trainium capacity, while OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, has agreed to consume about 2 gigawatts, with deployment beginning to ramp up in 2027.

When we zoom out a bit, and look at Amazon’s overall 3Q26 report, we see that the company’s AI exposure is clearly leading its growth. Amazon’s net revenue in Q3 was up 12% from 3Q25, and hit $201.9 billion; we should note that this figure was nearly $340 million below expectations. Of the total revenue, AWS’s $46 billion made up approximately 23%. Amazon’s EPS in the third quarter of $1.89 was down 6 cents per share from the year-ago period’s $1.95 figure. Amazon attributed the year-over-year earnings decrease primarily to $9.5 billion in pre-tax gains from its Anthropic investments recorded during the third quarter of 2025.

Once again, UBS is bullish on a major-name tech giant. Keirstead says of Amazon, “AI model and chip agnostic nature of AWS will help position Amazon shares as a defensive AI play and an AI enabler to enterprises scaling their AI investments in 2027+. These positives outweigh the impact on AWS growth from quarterly variability in the model API access revenue stream. In terms of our AWS estimates, we’re trimming our revs growth estimates (for 4Q26 to 41% from 42%, for 2027 to 43% from 48%) and our margin estimate (for 2027 to 40% from 45%). Amazon is now a very different business than even 2-3 years ago and the investment research process needs to change with it, to break from the past. The AWS cloud segment, while still only 23% of revs, represented 60% of Amazon’s y/y revs growth in 3Q26, 63% of EBIT dollars, likely 70%+ of capex, and Amazon’s AI/AWS narrative and outlook dominate the investor debate.”

Quantifying his stance on Amazon, the top-rated tech expert sets a Buy rating with a $340 price target that indicates his confidence in a 27% gain for the next 12 months.

Wall Street is also bullish on Amazon, and the stock has a solid Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 43 recent reviews with a decidedly lopsided split of 42 Buys to just 1 Hold. The stock’s trading price of $267.74 and average target price of $324.41 together suggest an upside of 21% on the one-year horizon. (See AMZN stock forecast)

data.title: Palo Alto Networks Stock Jumps as AI Cyber Threats Create New Growth Opportunity
data.description:
Shares of cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks (PANW) jumped on Thursday after the company lifted its annual outlook. Meanwhile, CEO Nikesh Arora warned that serious software vulnerabilities are being discovered at nearly seven times last year’s monthly average. This could benefit Palo Alto by increasing demand for its virtual patching and AI security services, which would help the company generate additional recurring revenue.

Arora explained on Wednesday that security teams are struggling to install software fixes fast enough. Meanwhile, a recent AI-assisted hacking campaign targeted at least 19 organizations, with attackers gaining unauthorized access to systems or data at 10 of them.

Researchers from Palo Alto’s Unit 42 division uncovered the operation, which took place during August and September. The attackers used an open-source AI tool called Cairn to carry out 25 operations. At one organization, more than one million personal records were exposed. The software could plan attacks and adjust its approach without requiring someone to oversee every step.

This creates another problem for businesses. Even when software developers release security updates, companies cannot always install them immediately without the risk of disruptions to their systems. Arora expects that the heavy workload associated with these updates could continue for at least another 18 months.

Catalysts That May Push the Stock Higher

The growing number of software vulnerabilities could increase demand for Palo Alto’s virtual patching service, which protects vulnerable systems while companies prepare permanent fixes. Palo Alto already serves nearly 70,000 network security customers, giving it a sizable existing customer base for the service.

Meanwhile, demand for AI security is already contributing to the company’s growth. Its Prisma AIRS product reached nearly $170 million in annual recurring revenue within five quarters of becoming available, with more than 1,000 customers using the platform. Furthermore, traffic generated by AI agents on Palo Alto’s network security platform increased about ninefold year-over-year.

Yesterday’s earnings provided additional evidence of strong cybersecurity spending. Fiscal first-quarter revenue grew by 39% to $3.44 billion, while next-generation security annual recurring revenue increased by 66% to $9.73 billion.

Risks to Watch Out For

However, the sevenfold increase refers to discovered software vulnerabilities, not successful cyberattacks. AI can also help security teams find weaknesses before hackers exploit them. Therefore, the longer-term effect on cybersecurity spending remains uncertain.

Additionally, Palo Alto faces competition from other security providers, and some customers may prefer upgrading their existing tools rather than purchasing additional services.

The company’s valuation is another consideration. Palo Alto trades at roughly 82 times the midpoint of its projected Fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share. This leaves less room for disappointing results if demand for its newer AI security products slows down.

Is PANW Stock a Good Buy?

Turning to Wall Street, TipRanks data shows that analysts have a Strong Buy consensus rating on PANW stock. This is based on 32 Buys and eight Holds assigned in the past three months. Furthermore, the average PANW price target of $423.43 per share implies 17.1% upside potential. (See PANW Stock Forecast).
